sources.locator: HTML Living Standard; living standard accessed 2026-07; provisions applicable to Figures and captions
sources.claim: Figure groups self-contained media or code with an optional figcaption that names or explains that content.

canonicalExplanation.summary: `<figure>` groups **self-contained content** — an image, chart, code sample or quote — with its `<figcaption>`, so the caption is formally tied to what it describes. The caption and the image's `alt` do **different jobs**: the caption is visible to everyone and adds context; alt replaces the image for people who can't see it. Don't use figure as a generic box for layout.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A tutorial shows a screenshot of an error message, with a caption underneath: "Figure 2: the TypeError appears on line 12." Is that enough for a blind learner? Not if the image has no alt — they get the caption but not what the screenshot shows. A code screenshot and its explanatory caption are wrapped in figure, while the image still has suitable alt text. In this lesson you'll create a semantically grouped figure and caption without using figure as a generic wrapper.

```predict
{"question": "A figure has a figcaption. Can the img inside skip its alt?", "options": ["Yes, the caption covers it", "No — the img still needs alt; the caption adds context, it doesn't replace the image"], "answer": 1, "why": "Captions and alt text have different jobs. Keep a suitable alt (or alt=\"\" only if the caption fully conveys the image)."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Relative and absolute URLs**, **Paragraph and inline meaning**, and **Images and alternative text**.

sections.heading: The model: one self-contained unit plus its caption
sections.body:
```html ``` | Piece | Job | |---|---| | `figure`. | groups a self-contained item that could be moved elsewhere. | | `figcaption`. | visible caption, first or last child of figure. | | `alt`. | text replacement for the image itself. | ```reveal {"prompt": "Is a code sample in `
` allowed inside a figure?", "answer": "Yes. Figures can hold code listings, quotes, diagrams or videos — anything referred to as a unit."}
```

sections.heading: Not a layout box

includes: Group an image, chart or code listing with figcaption in figure.
Keep alt text and captions doing their separate jobs.

outcomes: Create a semantically grouped figure and caption without using figure as a generic wrapper.

examples.title: A code screenshot with a caption
examples.situation: A code screenshot and its explanatory caption are wrapped in figure while the image still has suitable alt text.
walkthrough: **Wrap in figure:** the screenshot and caption form one self-contained unit.
**Explanatory caption:** "Figure 2: the TypeError appears on line 12 when a number is added to text."
**Still suitable alt text:** the img's alt reads the error message itself, so screen readers will render what the screenshot shows.
examples.result: Everyone gets the context from the caption, and screen-reader users also get the screenshot's content from alt.

examples.title: The figure-as-wrapper page
examples.situation: A landing page uses `<figure>` for hero sections, pricing cards and the footer.
walkthrough: None of these are self-contained illustrations referred to from the text.
Screen readers announce many meaningless "figure" regions.
Fix: use div (or section/aside where meaningful); keep figure for real illustrations with captions.
examples.result: Only genuine illustrations are figures, and the page's structure reads clearly.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Using figcaption means the nested image can omit its alt attribute.
misconceptions.correction: A caption provides visible context for everyone; alt replaces the image for people who can't see it. The image still needs alt that fits its purpose, unless the caption already conveys everything and alt="" is chosen deliberately.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "A code screenshot with a caption", what information would be lost without alt?

analogy.example: A figure is like a **museum exhibit**: the object, plus the label on the wall (figcaption). An audio guide (alt) describes the object itself for someone who can't see it — the wall label alone isn't a description.
limitations: Exhibits are physical; figures can be moved around a page.
Not every box in a museum is an exhibit — like layout divs.

remediation.explanation: Two questions: **Is this a self-contained item the text refers to? → figure.** **If the image were missing, what does the caption NOT say? → that goes in alt.**

recap.summary: To create a semantically grouped figure and caption, wrap self-contained illustrations, charts or code in figure with a figcaption, keep suitable alt on images because captions don't replace them, and never use figure as a generic wrapper.
